# UNIVARIATE {.unnumbered}



The graphs in this part show what the values in one column look like.[^univariate]

## Bar graphs

A [bar graph](bar_graphs.qmd) compares groups of data. Each group gets one bar, and the bar is long or high to show how many there are in that group.[^bar-length] The bars can stand up or run across.[^bar-orient] When the bars stand up, the names of the groups run along the foot of the graph, and the numbers run up the side.[^bar-axes] If the graph compares more than one set of data, a color for each set shows which bar is which, and a key on the side of the graph names the colors.[^bar-legend]


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_bar_graphs-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Histograms

A [histogram](histograms.qmd) shows where numbers fall along a number line.[^hist-spread] Each bar covers a short part of the line, and how high the bar is shows how many numbers fall in that part.[^bins] A bar graph has space between its bars, but a histogram has none, because the parts meet end to end.[^no-gaps] The values we found run along the foot of the graph, and how many fall in each part runs up the side.[^hist-axes]


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_histograms-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Frequency polygons

A [frequency polygon](frequency_polygons.qmd) shows where numbers fall, like a histogram, but with points joined by straight lines instead of bars.[^freqpoly] Each point stands over the middle of a part along the foot of the graph, as high as the number of values in that part, and lines join the points.[^midpoint] People often use it to compare where numbers fall in more than one set of data.[^fp-compare] A key at the top or side of the graph tells which line is which.[^fp-legend]


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_frequency_polygons-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Dot-plots

A [dot plot](dot_plots.qmd) shows each number as a dot along one line. Dot plots work well for small or middle sized sets of data, because they help us see the look of the data, close groups, places with no dots, and numbers far from the rest.[^dot-patterns] Each dot stands for one piece of data. With some data the dots build up over each group, and with other data they run out along a line.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_dot_plots-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Density plots

A [density plot](density_plots.qmd) shows where numbers fall, using a line instead of bars. A hill is a line that is high in the middle and low on both sides. A density plot puts a small hill over each number and adds the hills together into one line.[^kernel] The line is high where many numbers fall and low where few do. Density plots help us compare where numbers fall in different sets of data on the same graph, with a color for each line and a key on the side that names them.[^density-compare] All of the area under the line adds up to one.[^area-one]


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_density_plots-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Violin plots

A [violin plot](violin_plots.qmd) shows where numbers fall and how often each value comes up.[^violin-likely] It is like a box plot, but with a density plot turned on its side and shown on both sides of a center line.[^violin-kde] The violin is wide where a value comes up often and less wide where it comes up less.[^violin-width] We can use violin plots to compare where numbers fall across groups. They often hold a small box plot inside to show the middle number and the middle half of the data.[^violin-box]


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_violin_plots-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


## Box-plots

A [box plot](box_plots.qmd) shows the data with five numbers: the smallest, the number that one in four values fall under, the middle, the number that three in four values fall under, and the largest.[^five-num] The graph looks like a box with a line across it. The line is the middle number, and the box runs from the one in four mark to the three in four mark.[^quartiles] Lines run from the box out to the smallest and largest values that are not far from the rest.[^whiskers] Any numbers far from the rest show up as dots past the ends of those lines.[^outliers] Box plots help us find numbers far from the rest and compare groups of data.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](univariate_files/figure-html/part_box_plots-1.png){fig-align='center' width=60% height=60%}
:::
:::


[^univariate]: Univariate graphs, which visualize the distribution of a single variable (one column).

[^bar-length]: Each category is represented by a rectangular bar whose length or height varies with the quantity (count) it represents.

[^bar-orient]: Bar graphs can be vertical or horizontal.

[^bar-axes]: In a vertical bar graph, the `x` axis lists the categories and the `y` axis shows the measured quantities.

[^bar-legend]: When multiple variables are compared, colors or patterns differentiate them, and a legend (usually to the side) explains them.

[^hist-spread]: The distribution of a continuous numerical variable.

[^bins]: Each bar covers a range of values (a bin), and its height is the frequency of observations in that bin.

[^no-gaps]: Histograms have no gaps between bars because the bins cover a continuous interval.

[^hist-axes]: The `x` axis displays the range of the measured variable, and the `y` axis shows the frequency of observations.

[^freqpoly]: A frequency polygon displays a distribution like a histogram, using points connected by line segments instead of bars.

[^midpoint]: Each frequency is plotted above the midpoint of its bin on the `x` axis.

[^fp-compare]: Frequency polygons are commonly used to compare distributions across multiple sets.

[^fp-legend]: A legend differentiates the variables.

[^dot-patterns]: Dot plots suit small to moderate datasets and reveal patterns, clusters, gaps, and outliers.

[^kernel]: A kernel density estimate. A kernel (Gaussian by default in `geom_density()`) is placed over each value, and the kernels are summed into one smooth curve showing where values are concentrated.

[^density-compare]: Density plots compare the distributions of different datasets on one graph, using color to differentiate the curves and a legend to explain them.

[^area-one]: The total probability (the area under the density curve) is 1.

[^violin-likely]: Violin plots show the distribution and how likely each value is to occur (its probability density).

[^violin-kde]: Violin plots are similar to box plots, with a rotated kernel density plot mirrored on each side.

[^violin-width]: The width of the violin at each value shows its density; wider sections mean the value occurs more often.

[^violin-box]: An inner box plot shows the median and interquartile range (IQR).

[^five-num]: Box plots (box-and-whisker plots) use the five number summary: minimum, first quartile (25th percentile), median, third quartile (75th percentile), and maximum.

[^quartiles]: The line marks the median, and the box spans the first to the third quartile (the interquartile range).

[^whiskers]: The whiskers, which extend from the box to the most extreme values within 1.5 × IQR of the box.

[^outliers]: Outliers, plotted as individual points beyond the whiskers.
